title: Your bank connectivity strategy may be slowing revenue growth
summary: Fragmented bank connectivity drives up costs, complicates compliance, and slows growth. Learn how treasury can simplify payments and strengthen control.
body_markdown:
Bank connectivity is often treated as an infrastructure expense. But when fragmented connections create manual work, complicate compliance, and slow payment operations, the costs can extend far beyond IT. For corporate treasury teams, these inefficiencies consume resources, increase operational risk, and make it harder to support business growth.


The question isn’t simply whether your bank connections work. It’s whether they’re working efficiently enough to support the business.


## Fragmented connectivity creates hidden costs


For many organizations, bank connectivity has evolved one relationship at a time. A new bank, entity, acquisition, or market introduces another connection, format, portal, or process. Eventually, treasury is managing a patchwork of host-to-host connections,[SWIFT](https://www.opentext.com/what-is/swift) messaging, APIs, file transfers, banking portals, and manual workflows. Each connection may function perfectly well on its own. Together, they can create significant operational complexity.


Treasury and finance teams spend valuable time gathering payment information, reconciling transactions, investigating exceptions, and maintaining connections. As transaction volumes grow, so does the workload.


**More transactions shouldn’t automatically mean more manual work.** Yet without standardized processes, organizations can find themselves adding resources simply to maintain existing operations.


## Payment complexity can increase compliance costs


Every manual touchpoint creates another opportunity for error, inconsistent controls, or incomplete audit trails. When payments move between ERPs,[treasury management](https://www.opentext.com/what-is/treasury-management) systems, financial networks, and banks, fragmented workflows can make it difficult to apply consistent validation, approval, and monitoring processes.


Consider the potential consequences:


- **Inconsistent controls:** Different banks, systems, and payment processes may require separate validation and approval procedures.
- **Higher exception-handling costs:** Errors and rejected payments require investigation, correction, and sometimes reprocessing.
- **Difficult reconciliation:** Disconnected information makes it harder to match transactions, identify discrepancies, and demonstrate compliance.
- **Greater maintenance demands:** Changing bank requirements, payment formats, and standards can require additional IT effort.


These challenges don’t just increase costs. They can also weaken governance and make audit readiness more difficult.


Standardizing payment workflows and embedding controls directly into transaction processes can help reduce manual intervention while improving consistency and oversight.


## When payment operations slow down, business growth can suffer


The impact of inefficient connectivity doesn’t stop with treasury. Growth often introduces new banks, entities, currencies, payment requirements, and transaction volumes. If every expansion requires another custom integration or manual process, the cost and complexity of supporting the business increase. Payment delays and exceptions can also affect supplier relationships, business operations, and the timely movement of funds.


Meanwhile, resources devoted to maintaining fragmented connections aren’t available for higher-value activities. Better connectivity won’t generate revenue on its own. But reducing operational friction can help organizations control costs, support expansion, and put resources to more productive use.


## Simplify the flow without replacing core systems


Modernizing bank connectivity doesn’t have to mean replacing effective ERP or treasury management systems. A more centralized approach can connect existing systems with banking partners while standardizing payment processing, data transformation, validation, and exception management.


Solutions such as[OpenText Financial Hub](https://www.opentext.com/products/financial-hub) can help organizations simplify financial integration and payment workflows across systems and banking networks.


For treasury, the objective is straightforward: fewer manual touchpoints, more consistent controls, better payment visibility, and infrastructure that can adapt as the business changes.


## Make connectivity an advantage, not an expense


Your bank connectivity strategy should do more than keep payments moving. It should help control operational costs, strengthen governance, and support the business as it grows. By reducing fragmentation and standardizing payment processes, treasury can spend less time managing complexity and more time supporting financial and business priorities.
